name: Queen's Gambit
summary: Challenge Black's center with 1.d4 d5 2.c4. Learn how the Accepted, Declined and Slav change your plans, when to recover a pawn, and why development matters more than a tempting capture.

chunks.title: Introduction & Main Line
chunks.summary: The core move order 1.d4 d5 2.c4 and why it works: White attacks the d5 pawn from the side and asks Black how they want to defend the center.
keyIdeas: c4 attacks d5 with a flank pawn: exchanging it for Black's d-pawn leaves White with two central pawns against one.
Nc3 attacks d5 directly; Nf3 supports d4 and controls e5. Both develop, but they do different jobs.
Recognize Black's choice: ...dxc4 trades the center for activity, ...e6 supports d5 but blocks the c8 bishop, and ...c6 supports d5 while keeping that bishop's diagonal open.

line.note: Occupies d4, controls e5 and opens the c1 bishop's diagonal. The queen supports the pawn along the d-file.
Black occupies d5 and controls e4. White needs to challenge this central foothold.
Attacks d5 with the c-pawn. If ...dxc4 follows, Black's central pawn moves away, making a later e4 easier to arrange.

comparison.explanation: 2.Nc3 develops, but blocks your c-pawn. Playing c4 first challenges d5 immediately and keeps the Queen's Gambit structure available.

checkpoint.prompt: What should White challenge before developing the queenside knight?
checkpoint.answer: Black's d5 pawn. Play c4 first so the knight on c3 will not block this pawn break.

line.note: Supports d5 with another pawn and opens the f8 bishop's diagonal. The cost is restricting the c8 bishop behind e6.
Develops while adding a direct attack on d5. The c-pawn has already moved, so this knight no longer obstructs c4.

comparison.explanation: 3.Nf3 is also sound: it supports d4 and controls e5. Nc3 is our choice because it attacks d5 directly; it is not a forced move.

line.note: Develops a knight, reinforces d5 and controls e4. Black is preparing to bring out the f8 bishop and castle.
Attacks the f6 knight along the diagonal toward the queen. This relative pin creates pressure, but does not by itself win d5: the e6 pawn still defends it.

questions.prompt: You're White. Start the Queen's Gambit.
questions.hint: Push a center pawn that the queen already protects.
questions.explanation: 1.d4 takes space, opens the c1 bishop and starts every Queen's Gambit.

questions.prompt: Black matched you in the center. Offer the gambit.
questions.hint: Hit d5 from the side with a flank pawn.
questions.explanation: 2.c4 attacks d5 from the side. Compared with 2.Nc3, it keeps the c-pawn active. After ...dxc4, White can develop with Nf3 and e3, then usually recover with Bxc4.

questions.prompt: Black declined the gambit with 2...e6. Which developing move adds pressure to d5?
questions.explanation: 3.Nc3 develops and attacks d5 directly. 3.Nf3 is equally respectable, supporting d4 and controlling e5 instead. This course chooses Nc3 for immediate pressure, not because Nf3 is a mistake.

plans.white: Develop Nf3 and e3, bring out the f1 bishop and castle. Choose a central break only after checking Black's setup.
plans.black: Develop ...Be7 and castle; seek ...c5 or ...e5 to challenge d4 and release the cramped pieces.

chunks.title: Queen's Gambit Accepted
chunks.summary: Black takes on c4 and gives up the center for a while in exchange for free development. White's job is to win the pawn back calmly and keep a central advantage.
keyIdeas: Recover c4 as part of development with e3 and Bxc4; avoid chasing material with an exposed queen.
Nf3 controls e5, discouraging Black's freeing ...e5 break. It does not make ...e5 illegal.
Black's ...c5 attacks d4. Castle before committing the center, then decide whether to maintain the tension, exchange or advance.

line.note: Take central space and open the c1 bishop.
Black matches White's central claim.
Challenge d5 before developing the b1 knight.
Black exchanges a central foothold for a temporary extra pawn and room for the pieces. This is a sound defense, not a mistake.
Develops and controls e5, making Black's immediate central expansion less attractive. White can recover c4 after preparing the bishop.

comparison.explanation: The check can recover c4, but moves the queen early and gives Black developing replies such as ...Nc6. Nf3 improves a minor piece first. The immediate 3.e4 is also a sound, sharper system.

line.note: Attacks d5 and e4, develops toward castling, and restrains White's central expansion.
Opens the f1–c4 diagonal and reinforces d4. The bishop can now recover the pawn in one move.

checkpoint.prompt: How can you recover c4 while improving a piece?
checkpoint.answer: Play e3 to open the f1 bishop, then Bxc4. The pawn recovery should help development rather than distract from it.

line.note: Opens Black's f8 bishop and supports a later ...c5 challenge to d4.
Restores material and develops the bishop toward f7. This is efficient development, though it does not force Black to answer a new threat.
Challenges d4 before White can build a large center unopposed. Black is seeking active counterplay, not just defending.
Secures the king and brings the h1 rook toward the center. White leaves the pawn tension unresolved to keep options open.

comparison.explanation: Exchanging is legal, but gives up your d4 foothold and clarifies Black's central task. Castling preserves the choice. This is a plan preference, not a claim that every capture loses.

line.note: Prepares ...b5, gaining queenside space and attacking the bishop on c4. White must account for that tempo.

questions.prompt: Black accepted the gambit. What's the most flexible developing move?
questions.hint: Develop the knight that controls e5.
questions.explanation: 3.Nf3 develops and controls e5, discouraging ...e5. It fits our calm e3/Bxc4 setup. 3.e3 and 3.e4 are also sound systems; the latter claims more space and requires different preparation.

questions.prompt: Time to collect the gambit pawn.
questions.hint: The light-squared bishop now has a path to c4.
questions.explanation: 5.Bxc4 recovers the pawn while developing a piece. The bishop now looks toward f7, but this is not a forcing attack or a tempo gain: Black can continue normally with ...c5.

questions.prompt: Black hits your center with ...c5. What's the calm, principled reply?
questions.explanation: 6.O-O secures the king and activates the rook before resolving the center. An immediate exchange on c5 would give up the d4 foothold; castling keeps that choice for later. Black still has active counterplay with ...a6 and ...b5.

plans.white: Consider Qe2 and Rd1 after development. Watch ...b5; prepare e4 only when d4 and the king are secure.
plans.black: Use ...c5 against d4 and ...a6–b5 to gain time against the bishop. Complete development rather than trying to keep c4 at any cost.

chunks.title: Declined: Orthodox Defense
chunks.summary: Against ...e6, ...Be7 and ...Nbd7, develop without assuming the pin wins a pawn. Understand the timing of ...dxc4 and prepare for Black's central breaks.
keyIdeas: Bg5 makes the f6 knight less free to move; ...Be7 breaks the pin to the queen. Always count the pawn defenders too.
Rc1 improves the rook before committing the f1 bishop. Black often waits for Bd3 before ...dxc4 so that bishop must move again.
A space advantage needs development behind it. Finish with O-O and watch for Black's freeing ...c5 or ...e5.

line.note: Occupy d4 and control e5.
Black stakes a claim to d5 and e4.
Challenge the d5 pawn with a flank pawn.
Black reinforces d5 but restricts the c8 bishop.
Develop and attack d5.
Black develops and reinforces d5.
Creates a relative pin to the queen. Since e6 still protects d5, this is positional pressure rather than an immediate pawn win.

checkpoint.prompt: Does pinning the f6 knight mean d5 is free to capture?
checkpoint.answer: No. The e6 pawn still defends d5. A pin is one detail in a full count of attackers, defenders and tactical replies.

line.note: Interposes the bishop between g5 and d8, freeing the f6 knight to move without exposing the queen. It also prepares castling.
Supports d4 and opens the f1 bishop. The c1 bishop is already outside the pawn chain, so e3 does not trap it.
Black secures the king before opening the center.
Develops the kingside knight, supports d4 and controls e5. The f1 bishop still needs to develop before White can castle.
Develops the b8 knight without blocking the c-pawn. It adds support for ...c5 and ...e5, though it temporarily restricts the c8 bishop.
Places the rook on the file that may open after pawn exchanges. It is also a useful move before committing the f1 bishop.

comparison.explanation: 7.Bd3 is also a natural developing move. After ...dxc4 the bishop must move again. Rc1 makes a useful rook move first, but does not prevent Black from capturing on c4.

line.note: Reinforces d5 again. Black is solid but must still find activity for the c8 bishop.
Develops toward h7 and clears f1 for castling. Black can now gain a tempo against this bishop with ...dxc4.
Black releases the central tension after the bishop has moved: recapturing costs White another bishop move.
Restores material and keeps the bishop active. White still needs to castle; Black can challenge the center, so neither side has a forced advantage.

questions.prompt: Black defends d5 with the knight. Put pressure on that defender.
questions.hint: Pin the f6 knight to the queen.
questions.explanation: 4.Bg5 pins the knight that guards d5. That defines the classical Orthodox lines.

questions.prompt: Your f1 bishop is still at home. Which knight move supports d4 and prepares castling?
questions.hint: The kingside knight is still at home.
questions.explanation: 6.Nf3 develops the kingside knight, supports d4 and controls e5. The f1 bishop has not developed yet: Bd3 or Be2 and O-O still remain. Rc1 is a reasonable alternative move order.

questions.prompt: Black finally took on c4. Restore material.
questions.hint: Use the bishop on d3 to recover the pawn.
questions.explanation: 9.Bxc4 restores material. Black waited until Bd3 to capture, so White's bishop has moved twice. Rc1 was useful preparation for a future open c-file; White should now finish development with O-O.

plans.white: Castle, improve the queen and rooks, then look for e4 if supported. Do not rush pawn captures just because a knight appears pinned.
plans.black: Free the position with ...c5 or ...e5 when prepared; develop the c8 bishop after creating room.

chunks.title: Slav Defense
chunks.summary: Black supports d5 with ...c6 while keeping the c8 bishop's diagonal open. After ...dxc4, a4 discourages ...b5; recover c4, castle, and prepare e4 with support.
keyIdeas: ...c6 reinforces d5 while leaving the c8 bishop's diagonal open, but occupies the b8 knight's natural c6 square.
After ...dxc4, a4 controls b5 and makes it harder for Black to maintain the extra pawn with ...b5. It also weakens b4.
After recovering c4, castle and prepare e4 with care. Black's ...Bb4 pins Nc3 and directly contests that plan.

line.note: Occupy the center with d4.
Black occupies d5.
Challenge d5 and offer the c-pawn.
Supports d5 without placing a pawn on e6, so the c8 bishop can leave the back rank.
Supports d4 and controls e5 while keeping the b1 knight flexible.
Black develops and increases control of e4.
Adds pressure on d5. Now both white knights influence the center.
Black captures after developing a knight. The extra pawn may be supported by ...b5 if White allows it.
Controls b5, making it harder to support c4 with ...b5. The cost is leaving b4 less well controlled by White's pawns.

comparison.explanation: 5.e3 develops the bishop's diagonal immediately, but allows ...b5 to support c4 and gain space. Our 5.a4 addresses that specific threat first; it does weaken b4.

checkpoint.prompt: What is Black hoping to do before you recover c4, and what square can you control to interfere?
checkpoint.answer: Black wants ...b5 to support c4. The move a4 controls b5, at the price of weakening b4.

line.note: Develops the c8 bishop before ...e6 can shut its diagonal. It also controls e4, the square White wants to occupy.
Opens the f1 bishop's diagonal to c4 and reinforces d4. The tradeoff is temporarily restricting White's c1 bishop.
Supports the center and releases the f8 bishop. Black's light-squared bishop is already outside the pawn chain.
Recovers the pawn and develops toward f7. White has a d- and e-pawn against Black's e-pawn in the center, but still must prepare e4.
Pins Nc3 to the king, making it harder for that knight to help an e4 advance. The b4 square became available after a4.
Removes the absolute pin on Nc3 and secures the king. Qe2 may help prepare e4, but check Black's pressure before pushing.

questions.prompt: The Slav. What's the most flexible developing move?
questions.explanation: 3.Nf3 develops while keeping options open. It also covers e5 and d4.

questions.prompt: Black took on c4 and wants to hold it with ...b5. Stop that plan.
questions.hint: A rook-pawn move puts a stop to ...b5.
questions.explanation: 5.a4 controls b5 and makes ...b5 harder to sustain, so e3 and Bxc4 can recover c4 in the main line. This is not a permanent ban on ...b5: pawn breaks depend on tactics. Also notice the weakened b4 square, which Black can use with ...Bb4.

questions.prompt: Your bishop's diagonal is open. Recover c4 while developing.
questions.hint: e3 opened a diagonal for your bishop.
questions.explanation: 7.Bxc4 restores material and develops toward f7. It does not gain a forcing tempo. After ...Bb4, castle to remove the pin on Nc3, then prepare Qe2 and e4 only if the center is supported.

plans.white: Use Qe2 and piece support to prepare e4. Watch pressure on c3 and d4 rather than assuming the central advance works automatically.
plans.black: Use ...Bb4 and ...Bf5 to restrain e4. Castle and look for a timely ...c5 or ...e5 break.

chunks.title: Exchange: From Opening to Plan
chunks.summary: Trade on d5 to reach the Carlsbad structure. Learn when a minority attack makes sense and why a pawn break needs preparation.
keyIdeas: After cxd5 exd5, the pawn structure changes. A plan that works here does not automatically work in the Accepted or Slav.
White can prepare b4–b5 to undermine c6 and create a target on the c-file; this aims at weak pawns, not checkmate.
Finish development first. Black can use ...Ne4 and kingside activity while White prepares queenside play.

line.note: Occupy the center.
Black establishes d5.
Challenge d5 with the flank pawn.
Reinforce d5 with e6.
Develop and attack d5.
Develop and reinforce d5.
Exchange the c-pawn for Black's d-pawn to clarify the structure.

comparison.explanation: 4.Nf3 maintains the tension and is sound. cxd5 chooses a clearer pawn structure; it does not win material because ...exd5 restores it.

line.note: The e-pawn replaces the d-pawn on d5. White now has two queenside pawns (a and b) against Black's three (a, b and c): the structure behind a possible minority attack.
Develop outside the future e3 pawn chain and place a relative pin on Nf6.
Break the pin and prepare to castle.
Support d4 and release the f1 bishop.
Secure the king.
Develop toward h7 and prepare castling.
Develop without blocking the c-pawn; ...c6 can reinforce d5.
Support d4 and clear g1 for castling. A setup with Nge2 is another sound plan, but this lesson uses Nf3.
Support d5 with a pawn. The c6 pawn may later become a target after a b4–b5 break.
Secure the king before beginning a flank operation.

checkpoint.prompt: Should White start b4 immediately or secure the king first?
checkpoint.answer: Castle first in this setup. A minority attack takes several moves; White needs king safety and developed pieces before investing time on the flank.

line.note: Put the rook on the e-file and prepare central piece activity. Black can answer queenside play with pressure in the center or on the kingside.

plans.white: Consider Rc1, Qc2, Rab1 and b4–b5 if Black cannot create stronger central threats. A supported e4 break is another plan, not an automatic move.
plans.black: Watch the b5 break, seek ...Ne4 and improve the c8 bishop. If White spends many tempi on the flank, create central or kingside activity.

questions.prompt: Choose the pawn exchange that reaches the Carlsbad structure.
questions.hint: Exchange your c-pawn for Black's d-pawn.
questions.explanation: 4.cxd5 exd5 changes the structure without winning a pawn. Keeping the tension with Nf3 is also sound; the exchange gives us a clear structure to study.

questions.prompt: Black recaptured with the e-pawn. Develop your c1 bishop before e3 restricts it.
questions.explanation: 5.Bg5 develops outside the future pawn chain and puts pressure on Nf6. After ...Be7, White will play e3 and Bd3. Bf4 is another sound square.

questions.prompt: You want a future b4–b5 break. What should you complete first?
questions.explanation: 9.O-O completes king safety before a slow queenside operation. Later b4–b5 aims to weaken c6; it is not an immediate attack on the king. Always check Black's central counterplay first.

chunks.title: Traps & Pitfalls
chunks.summary: Two classic traps. One punishes Black for greedily holding the gambit pawn. The other is a trap White must not fall into when d5 looks loose.
keyIdeas: If Black holds c4 with ...b5, a4 undermines the chain. Then Qf3 uses the long diagonal to hit the a8 rook.
The Elephant Trap: after cxd5 exd5, Nxd5?? loses to ...Nxd5!, because Bxd8 is met by ...Bb4+ and Black comes out a piece ahead.
Pins work both ways. Before you grab a pawn, check whether your own pieces are overloaded.

line.note: Begin with central space.
Black occupies d5.
Offer c4 to draw the d-pawn away.
Black accepts the pawn; this alone is a sound choice.
Opens the f1 bishop so Bxc4 is possible.
Tries to keep c4 with a pawn chain. Black is spending time on pawns while the pieces remain at home.
Attacks the supporting b5 pawn. If Black pushes ...b4, the support of c4 disappears and Bxc4 becomes possible.
Reinforces b5, but leaves a tactical weakness on the f3–a8 diagonal once the pawns exchange.
Removes b5's current occupant and forces Black to reconsider the chain.
Restores the chain, but vacates c6. The f3–e4–d5–c6–b7–a8 diagonal is now open.
Attacks the rook on a8. For example, ...Nc6 blocks the diagonal but allows Qxc6+, winning a knight. The early queen move is justified by a concrete tactic.

comparison.explanation: 6.Bxc4 is a normal recovery, but misses the chance to win a piece. Qf3 is stronger here because the opened diagonal creates a concrete threat to Ra8.

checkpoint.prompt: What changed when Black's c-pawn left c6? Is an early queen move justified now?
checkpoint.answer: The diagonal from f3 to a8 opened. Qf3 attacks a rook, so this queen move creates a concrete threat rather than merely hoping for an attack.

questions.prompt: Black is trying to keep the extra pawn with ...b5. Punish it.
questions.hint: Attack the b5 pawn, the base of the chain.
questions.explanation: 4.a4 undermines the b5–c4 chain at once. Black's queenside starts to come apart.

questions.prompt: Black's queenside pawns have gone. Find the move that wins material.
questions.hint: Look at the long light-squared diagonal toward a8.
questions.explanation: 6.Qf3! hits the a8 rook along the open diagonal. Black has to give up material, for example 6...Nc6 7.Qxc6+.

questions.prompt: d5 looks like it's hanging because the f6 knight is pinned. Is it? Play the correct move.
questions.hint: Don't take on d5. Just keep developing.
questions.explanation: 6.e3 or 6.Nf3 continues development safely. The tempting 6.Nxd5?? fails to ...Nxd5! 7.Bxd8 Bb4+ 8.Qd2 Bxd2+ 9.Kxd2 Kxd8, leaving Black a piece ahead. The f6 knight is relatively pinned to the queen, not absolutely pinned to the king: a forcing check changes the calculation.

plans.white: If Black abandons the extra pawn, recover it and develop. If Black tries to hold it, calculate forcing threats before sending the queen out.
plans.black: Prefer development and central counterplay to defending c4 with more pawn moves. In the Elephant Trap, a relative pin can be broken with a forcing check.
